text: Chapter 1 introduced Secure Data Sharing as a way to give another account read access to your data. This lesson covers what Snowflake built on top of that idea: a way to share application logic — Snowpark code, Streamlit apps, stored procedures — not just raw tables, and even sell it.

A provider can package a Streamlit app, stored procedures, and functions written in Snowpark, JavaScript, or SQL, and ship all of it as something a consumer installs and runs inside their own account — with versioning, patches, and structured logging built in, none of which plain data sharing gives you.

Once a provider publishes a listing, a consumer installs the app, and it becomes a genuine Snowflake Native App running inside the consumer's own account. The consumer's data stays inside their own account the entire time — the framework is built so a provider's logic can run against a consumer's data without the provider ever needing standing access to see it directly.

Everything a Native App needs is bundled into an application package. The manifest file defines the app's configuration, including where the setup script lives. The setup script is a SQL script that runs automatically on install or upgrade — it's what actually creates the app's tables, Streamlit app, and stored procedures inside whichever account installs it.

This is what a consumer actually gets: a real application, not a data export. A published listing can go to specific named accounts, or out to the full Snowflake Marketplace, free or paid — the real monetization path Native Apps open up that plain data sharing never offered.

That closes Chapter 18. You've gone from Snowpark DataFrames running inside Snowflake's engine, to UDFs and stored procedures making that logic callable and schedulable, to the Native App Framework packaging all of it into something a provider can install, version, and sell.
